title: China’s View of the War in Iran: A Conversation with Zhang Chuchu
transcriptText:
Welcome to China Power. I'm Bonnie Lin,
[music] your host, and in this podcast,
we dissect critical issues underpinning
China as a global power.
>> [music]
>> Today, I am joined by Dr. John Chuchu,
an associate professor at the School of
International Relations and Public
Affairs, and Deputy Director at the
Center for Middle Eastern Studies at
Fudan University. In this episode, we'll
explore how China views the war in Iran,
and what the conflict means for China's
interests and strategy in the region.
Chuchu, thank you for joining me.
>> Thank you for having me.
>> So, I like to start off with this teaser
question of uh Chuchu, when you look at
the last year, what have you found most
interesting or most surprising when
looking at China's relationship with the
Middle East?
>> Um over the past year, um
okay, I would say um
uh a lot of things have actually
happened, and um of course, I I think
the depths of the relations between um
China and the Middle East have been
largely strengthened. Um right now, I
would say there are a lot of sectors
uh of cooperation. In the past, people
often thought that, okay, China was only
a big importer of Middle Eastern energy,
including natural gas and um oil. But,
currently, um there are obviously a lot
of cooperation in different fields, such
as digital economy, infrastructure,
um also renewable energies. And um at
the same time, China is not only an
importer of oil from the region, but
also China is a big investor. But, at
the same time, the uh Middle Eastern um
national sovereign funds have also
invested a lot in China. So, I would say
this kind of cooperation is more uh
multi-layered. And um last but not
least, I often I also see that there are
a lot of new mechanism of cooperation
between China and the Middle East. Well,
in the past, we often say that um the
two sides cooperated with each other
through bilateral means and also
multilateral means. But at the same
time,
today, for instance, last year,
there was the summit of ASEAN, Gulf and
China.
So it means that China and the Middle
Eastern region
are involving with each other in
different ways.
>> So would you say from your perspective
you've been surprised at how deep
China's relationship is with the Middle
East and how much is it has expanded in
the last year?
>> Indeed, that is what I think.
>> Great. Thank you. And I think that's a
good segue to focus on the topic that we
want to discuss, which is China's view
of the war in Iran. So maybe let's start
off just at the larger picture. From
your perspective, how is China viewing
the war overall?
Are there any
main
trends or themes in terms of how Chinese
officials or Chinese scholars are
discussing the war and its overall
impacts?
>> Right. Of course, I think everybody
today is following the news and is very
concerned with what's going on in Iran.
And actually, it's not just a war in
Iran, but also it has a lot of spillover
effects. So as for China, the first
issue is the spillover effect
that
concerns a lot of people here.
I was say today, yes, you can see
Lebanon is involved and also Iraq. And
at the same time,
the Gulf states have also been involved
in this conflict. So right now, it's not
just a conflict between the United
States, Israel, and Iran, but also a
conflict that has
obvious spillover effect in the whole
region. So that is what makes things
worse.
And at the same time, I think China is
also very concerned about
how the war
happened at the very beginning because
absolutely this is a war that violates
the international law and undermines
regional stability.
Well, I believe that the escalating
conflict between
Iran and the United States is
a concern not only just for China, but
also for the entire international
community
because when national sovereignty is
violated, when the seriousness of
international negotiations diminishes,
and when international law and force are
disregarded, it means that the
international community may face more
conflicts in the future. And the liberal
international order will be undermined.
And another very dangerous signal is
that
you know, at the very beginning in
February, there were a lot of people
asking the question of whether there was
there is going to be a war.
But in any case, the issue here is that
the United States and Iran were
negotiating with each other.
And at that time, there were a lot of
good news
talking about
the potential achievements that could be
accomplished through this kind of
negotiations, but in the end, there was
the war. So, in that case, a lot of
people might ask the question about
whether there would be trust between
different countries in the future. And I
think if
there is going to be less and less trust
between different states in the future,
then there that is going to be another
big challenge facing
the international society.
>> Thank you. Maybe we can go back and
unpack a number of points that you made.
So, you first mentioned that for China,
the largest issue is the spillover
effect. Um when it comes to spillover
effect, then you mentioned the um
the challenges to national sovereignty
and what that means in terms of under
in terms of undermining both regional
stability as well as how other countries
may use force elsewhere.
Is there a concern that
um when you refer to other countries
um that it's not just the United States,
but potentially
a range of countries could be taking
lessons learned from this to allow them
to use force
in different contexts or what what
exactly is the concern here in terms of
from China's perspective?
>> Okay, so there is a negotiation, so we
may not so right. So we are negotiating
with each each other, but right now
suddenly um the the top leader of one
country who is in charge of the big
um decision-maker
in this kind of negotiation of one
country, and he could be attacked. So um
if I mean more and more countries follow
the suit and follow um this kind of
actions, then of course it's going to
send a very dangerous signal.
Uh and another thing that I want to
point out is the uh lose of trust
between different countries.
Um as we have just discussed, um in the
past, you know,
why were there um different, you know,
alliances, international organizations,
um and it was also international norms.
Um and one big purpose is that different
countries wished to solve their problems
and differences through this this kind
of mechanisms. But today, if there is no
longer enough trust between different
states, then more and more states um
might want to um resort to
um you know, weapons or like the
military operations to confront each
other when they have problems with each
other. And my concern is that at the
moment this might be a new trend in the
Middle East um because right now, you
know, the confrontation
between Iran and the Gulf countries are
there. So in this kind of context when
the countries
um might resort to
um you know, military confrontation and
might
uh even trigger a arm race uh between
different countries.
>> Uh so just to make sure your concern
about the lack of trust in negotiations
only applies to the Middle East or does
that apply more broadly? Uh as you know,
um the United States and China have um
planned to increase communications with
each other this year. Does it also apply
from your perspective in terms of
US-China relations as in there are more
folks uh in China wary of what the
United States is saying and uh how much
they can trust the United States?
>> All right. Um first the first thing is
that um
as for the relations between China and
the United States, um my perspective is
that um both states are big powers in
the world today and I think um the way
how
they interact with each other depends on
the bilateral relations but not what's
going on in the other parts of the
world.
Um so I don't think um the relations are
going to be changed much um due to this
war um right. Um but as you have
mentioned, if this is a trend
uh of the trust uh you know, the the the
loss of trust um between different
states. So right now it's occurring in
the Middle East uh but at the same time
it might have a spillover effect uh that
might affect the mindset of the other
countries as well.
>> What from your perspective are some of
the economic spillover effects if any?
>> All right, of course there are many
actually and that is a big concern for
China and as well as a lot of other
countries.
For example, there is the problem of the
disruption
of the international oil supply at the
moment and you know for China for
instance, China is a big importer of oil
and also today
you know China is developing its
industry and also China is a leading
buyer of oil from the region.
While major the Belt and Road Initiative
investments including energy
infrastructure, ports, railways and
connectivity corridors in major
countries in the Middle East. So of
course what's going on in the Middle
East has a an impact on China's economic
cooperation
with the region. And on the other hand,
the rising oil price is another big
concern. China is a major oil and also
LNG importer from the region.
As you can see right now China cannot
get enough LNG from Qatar for instance
and also China's energy security would
be severely impacted if it could not
secure stable oil supply.
And furthermore, a fluctuation in
international oil prices could also
seriously affect China's price levels
and economic development. So of course
this kind of spillover effect
has a big impact on China.
>> As you look at the overall impacts,
geopolitical and economic from China's
perspective, are we witnessing a turning
point now in um
in the international order?
>> In changing international dynamics,
um, think well there are some changes,
but before that, uh um, what I want to
add is that, uh, for China itself, um, I
think this spillover effect is there,
uh, and it's becoming increasingly
apparent, um, but at the same time, I
would say it's not, um, just create a
triggering an impact on China, but also
many other countries.
Um, for instance, um, Singapore, South
Korea, Japan, and Europe as big, uh, and
important, um, energy importers, they
have also been highly impacted, um, by,
um, the, uh, energy, uh,
supply shortage, and also by the
fluctuation of oil prices,
um, but I would say at the same time,
China has demonstrated, um, strong
resilience and the ability to withstand,
um, risks. Um, so, um, because China has
strategic reserves sufficient to
weather, um, multi-months disruptions,
and also China always seeks to increase
its oil supply channels to,
um, ensure its energy security, and also
in recent years China has been
promoting, um, energy transition. Um,
the development of new energy sources
also helps alleviate the, um, impact of
disruptions to, um, the global energy
supply chain. Um, so, um,
uh,
um, just now we have discussed like what
could be the, um, impact of this war,
um,
on the global or international order.
Um, I would say, um, so far we have not
yet seen, um, how the war is going to
end itself, so it's very hard to say,
but so far what we have seen is that,
um, first of all, it has a great impact
on the Middle Eastern, um, order,
because as I have just mentioned, it
seems that more and more countries are
becoming um, um unstable. And if you
have like more and more vacuum in this
region,
um a lot of countries, uh for instance,
if they they face instability,
um then it means that in the future,
um there might be a rise of um for
instance, um different armed groups in
the region. Um so, that is another
concern. Um and at the same time, uh I
would say um right now because the Gulf
countries and Iran, they have confronted
with each other, so that is another
variable regarding the regional order.
And in terms of international order, um
I think today what I have observed is
that um the big power politics
um have risen because currently um the
conflict also uh is is spillover effect
uh has a great impact on uh
most of the countries in the world, I
would say. But at the same time, I would
say the big powers, um since they have
more
oil reserves, so they demonstrate um
strong resilience um in this kind of
period.
>> And it seems like part of what you're
saying there is that the U.S. and China
as two bigger powers are still
negatively impacted by the war in Iran,
but still probably doing relatively
better than smaller powers. Is that a
correct uh interpretation of that
statement?
>> So, if we talk about the impact of this
conflict, we can see that the majority
of countries have already been touched
and affected by this war, right?
Especially when it comes to the
fluctuation of oil price and also the
uh uh
the the disruption of the energy supply.
I think for smaller countries, there are
two very big challenges. The first one
is instability, because as you can see,
for instance, in the Middle East,
a lot of countries have already been
tracked or involved into this war, and
the attractiveness
as important
investment
destinations
have gradually
losing their attractiveness. So, of
course, that is a great impact. And as
for a lot of big powers,
then
since there is stability, so that is a a
difference. And another big issue here
is about the economic impact, because
for example, for
smaller powers, since they have
limited
economic resilience,
and also they have limited oil reserves,
so it means that the economic resilience
is limited. But as for the big powers,
for example, I think the um
I think the interests are more
multi-layered. For example, as for
China, well, China is a big importer of
oil and gas, but at the same time,
China also has
quite strong oil reserves,
so that might help solve part of the
problem. And as for the United States,
well, the United States
it is a very important oil exporter
at the same time. So, although I have
many friends living in the United States
saying that they are facing the problem
of the increasing gasoline price, but at
the same time for the whole country of
the United States, right now they can
export their oil to
the oil importers in the world. So, I
don't think
for the United States is um
is only a negative impact.
Uh and as for Russia today, a lot of
people saying that Russia is a winner
because right now
because in over the past few years
you know, Russia faced the economic
sanctions, but today
you know, even the United States asks
Russia to sell more oil
to the market.
So, in that sense, if you make a
comparison,
you will find that there is a very
different situation for different
countries at
at this moment.
>> So, as you talk about how these major
power big powers have more more oil
reserves and it seems like what you're
saying is the competition is also
rising.
Is this a move from I guess what China
has long said was a trend towards
multipolarity towards
um back to I don't know, bipolarity?
Like how do you how do you put this in
the context of what China has long
assessed to be that the world order is
moving towards multipolarity?
>> Well, I think that multipolarity is
there and that is of course the trend
because currently you see what's going
in the Middle East
after this conflict erupted, a lot of
countries they have expressed their
ideas and I think it's not just this
war, but actually
ever since the Gaza war
erupted, um
you know, a lot of countries in the
global south they have tried to make
their voice unheard instead of just
passively accept
what's going on. Right? So, so I think
right, there is the trend of
multipolarity, of course.
And at the same time Um, this war we can
also see that different countries, they
are also trying to express the different
voices and even regarding the position,
for instance,
um, there is a big difference between
the United States um, position and the
European
um, positions.
Um, so, um, in any case, I think, um,
right, the multi-polarity
trend
um, has not been weakened in any case.
>> I'd like to now move to a uh, slightly
related question, which is looking at
how Chinese experts, not necessarily the
Chinese government, look at the war.
Are there different perspectives within
China's academic and policy circles
about the war and what approach China
should take towards the war?
>> Um, not really, actually, at least from
my own observation, because, um,
currently,
um, if I follow, um,
what um, the experts and the
scholars, um, they have expressed today,
I think that, in fact, I have seen a lot
of consensus
um, between them,
um, because, um, for instance, I think
most of the experts here, um, they agree
um, that uh, there is this very strong
necessity
uh, for countries like China to develop
the renewable energy
um, to promote
um, the energy transition, because right
now you can see that if you just um,
depend on
um, the uh,
the the fossil fuels, for instance, then
there is a high risk and also it's very
important to diversify your energy
supply and also
um, the transportation
um, routes of the energy. Um, so, that
is a very big consensus and I would say
another consensus is that um,
a lot [clears throat] of experts have
also seen that it's very important right
now to de-escalate this conflict because
as we have mentioned there are a lot of
spillover effects and also
that is triggering
the
And also at the same time this conflict
has already
triggered a lot of negative impacts on
the global economy
and if the conflict just continue like
that maybe the oil price can also reach
to let's say 200
dollars per barrel and that is even
going to trigger a very severe economic
crisis in the whole world. So I think
right now in the academic community in
China
I think the consensus is that
the different parts they need to
negotiate with each other and
de-escalate the conflict as soon as
possible.
>> So going back to what we were discussing
in terms of the consensus within China.
You mentioned two areas of consensus.
You mentioned the second one being
China's desire to de-escalate the
conflict. Is there also consensus or
agreement among Chinese experts on how
China should de-escalate or be involved
in the de-escalation?
>> [clears throat]
>> Okay, I think first of all
this conflict is not initiated by China
and the course of conflict at the moment
it mainly depends on the United States,
Israel and Iran.
Well yes, China is a big power
but I think what it can do is usually
limited when it comes to a conflict that
is not initiated by China. You know in
the past people often
you know when when there was the Gaza
war for instance
I've heard a lot of people making a
comparison between China's role and nice
States role and my answer
for them is that it's completely
different because
the United States was a very big
participant in that war whereas China
was not so of course you cannot compare
the two things and you cannot say okay
China you should solve a conflict that
is not initiated
by China
and at the same time regarding what
China can do at
this point China has
always advocated non-interference in the
internal affairs of the other countries
so in the Middle East China has
consistently adhered to the three nose
principle which means no proxies no fear
of influence and no feeling of power
vacuums so for China it always says that
okay if you cannot make a contribution
to the region's development at least you
should not destroy the region and play a
destructive role
so so far I think the efforts made by
China is that it's trying to make more
high-level diplomatic engagement for
example the foreign minister Wang Yi has
conducted
a lot of phone calls with counterparts
in the region and and I have talked to
different
counterparts in different countries
and also there is a dispatch of special
envoy for instance China sent special
envoy Zhai Jun to the Middle East in
early March
for shuttle diplomacy there
and also in April
as you can see the UAE Crown Prince
visited China and there was a talk
between
the UAE Crown Prince and President Xi.
And also President Xi put forward a
comprehensive four-point proposal
that offers, you know, a clear framework
of China to resolve the crisis.
>> Can you just elaborate a little bit more
on the three no's that you mentioned? I
think that might not be familiar to all
of my listeners. Where did the three
no's come from?
>> Oh, sure. Yes. So, for China, it has
always insisted on the principle of
three no's
in the Middle East. And it means, first
of all, no proxies because people often
say that today the
Middle Eastern people cannot decide
their own destiny because there are so
many
extra regional powers here.
And you can see that they try to support
different armed groups as proxies to
fight against each other. And that is
one important reason why you see so many
wars in the Middle East. And for China,
it always advocates that it's not going
support any proxies in the region. And
the second no is no sphere of influence.
A lot of commentators say that
the Middle East
has so many instabilities. And one
reason is that different countries, they
are trying to say, "Okay, this is my
backyard. This is your backyard." And
because the region is full of oil and
gas and a lot of resources, that is why
so many countries
seek this kind of influence. But as for
China, it has no intention
of creating this kind of sphere of
influence in the region. And also, you
can see that China does not have any
military bases in the region.
So, this is another principle of China.
And And third principle is no
no feeling of power vacuum because in
the past people often
often perceived the region of the Middle
East as through the lens of big power
politics and people often said that okay
there was a competition between China
and United States in the region
and there was even a saying that the
United States wished to decrease this
investment and the energy it put
in the region of the Middle East and
that is how China could come
and maybe become a new hegemon or
something but actually China has made it
very clear that it doesn't have this
kind of intention and it has no
intention to fill the so-called power
vacuum.
>> So you mentioned
the three no's principles that China has
for the Middle East
which I understand to be what Xi Jinping
laid out 2016 and you also mentioned
Xi Jinping's recent four-point proposal
as well as a number of perspectives from
the Chinese side on why China should
de-escalate but one thing that we've
also seen reported
in the Western media
and based on US intelligence sources is
that there was a debate or at least
consideration on China's end
to provide air defense weapons to Iran.
I don't know if that's true and I don't
know if you can comment on it but I've
also seen Chinese scholars such as Jin

future China should think about
providing military assistance to close
friends such as Iran. How popular is his
view and to what extent is there a
debate among
Chinese strategists
that as Beijing becomes more powerful
and needs to help its close friends
more.
>> Okay, thanks so much for this very
interesting question. Well, first of
all, I have to admit that I
have not seen this comment
from Sun Rong and I have not heard about
the news of supporting AD funds.
But well, I would say
there have always been diverse voices in
Chinese academia.
But in general, when it comes to this
US-Israeli war with Iran,
I think it's very interesting
if we say
will China provide military assistance
to close friends. Who is China's
friends? Iran is a friend, but also
Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates,
they're also very close friends of
China. Actually, China has a non-aligned
policy.
So, China
does not have any military ally.
And China has also consistently adhered
to a neutral stance in the Middle East
and it tries to maintain good relations
with all of the Middle Eastern
countries. And right now, what makes
things complicated is that
it has involved so many actors at the
moment, right? And even Saudi Arabia,
United Arab Emirates,
Bahrain for instance, they have their
their relations with Iran have
deteriorated. So, currently I think
China has considered consistently tried
to maintain
friendly relations with all of the
Middle Eastern countries
and is not trying to say, "Okay, I am
going to take sides
in this situation."
>> So, Choo Choo, you mentioned the
spillover effects and the impact the war
has
on China. It seems like what you're
saying right now is in the short term,
bigger powers like China and the United
States are
are impacted by the war, but the impact
is still relatively limited.
But if the war were to drag on, what are
some of the assessments
that you have or other Chinese have
analysts have about the longer-term

>> Mhm. Okay, thanks so much. Um,
of course, so um, whether it's long-term
or short-term, there is this war and
right now, um, it already has triggered
a lot of negative impacts on the whole
world. Mhm. I am not trying to say,
okay, the big powers do not have any
problems,
um, and everybody, um, is concerned with
what's going on. Let's say, um, the if
there is even an escalation of this
conflict and if it continues like that
for months, then that is going to be a
disaster, not only just for the Middle

the first issue here is that the oil
price can go even higher and if the oil
price, um,
reaches, um, $200 um, per barrel, then
it means that it's going to trigger a
global economic crisis and we can feel
inflation,
uh, in our country, for instance.
Um, also, um, the price
um, of a lot of, um, products uh, are
going to rise. So, of course, it's going
to affect, um, everybody's, um, daily
life.
And [snorts] the second issue here is

East. So, if the war just continue like
that, then it means that,
um, a lot of countries will a lot a lot
of people will become homeless and more
and more civilian in
will be destroyed and also you can see a
refugee
flows in the region. And also maybe in

And third,
if, you know, the war continues, then it
means that maybe the Hormuz crisis

have a great impact on the
international trade.
So, and also the international supply
chains. So, I think in general,
of course, for China, it doesn't want to
see
this kind of scenario happening.
>> Great, thank you.
Uh Duju, when you when Chinese analysts

there a consensus
in terms of
how and when the war will end? For

leverage
at this stage
and that is why it's unwilling to

stability in the Middle East in recent
years,
the
resulting deterioration of the security

at this stage.

to what extent do these dynamics

>> [snorts]
>> Right. So, first of all, um

relations between China and Iran
to a great extent. About the Hormuz

um more and more complicated at this

we should also look at what are the root

for this issue at the moment.
in China we have a saying that true bill

the I think the fundamental issue here
